C005.subject: raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets with high concentrations of fast-food franchises
C005.object: unemployment among teenage workers more than in other low-wage sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets with high concentrations of fast-food franchises unemployment among teenage workers more than in other low-wage sectors]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) study on the New Jersey minimum wage increase and its effects on fast-food employment — This classic natural experiment directly examines the impact of a minimum wage hike on fast-food sector employment, providing a benchmark for comparing teenage unemployment effects in high fast-franchise-density markets versus other low-wage sectors.

[PATH:literature] Cengiz et al. (2019) meta-analysis of minimum wage effects on low-wage employment, with subgroup analysis by industry and age group — This comprehensive review synthesizes evidence across many studies and can isolate the differential impact on teenage workers in fast-food-concentrated areas, helping to confirm or refute the hypothesized greater unemployment effect.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation model of a low-wage labor market with heterogeneous firms (e.g., monopsony vs. competitive) and teenage labor supply elasticity — A structural model parameterized to reflect high fast-food franchise density can test whether substitution effects, firm pricing power, or labor demand elasticity produce larger teenage unemployment compared to other low-wage sectors, offering causal predictions to guide empirical work.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with high fast-food franchise density

C006.subject: raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets unemployment among teenage workers]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of U.S. state-level minimum wage increases from 2000-2020, focusing on teenage employment rates in low-wage sectors (e.g., retail, food services) within 1-2 years post-implementation. — Provides direct, time-bound, and geographically relevant evidence on the short-term effect of minimum wage changes on teenage unemployment, allowing for causal inference through difference-in-differences or event-study designs.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on minimum wage effects on teenage employment, particularly those examining short-run elasticities in low-wage labor markets. — Synthesizes findings from multiple studies to assess the overall direction and magnitude of the effect, addressing the disputed status by weighing evidence from varying methodologies and time periods.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching labor market model calibrated to U.S. low-wage sectors, simulating the impact of a minimum wage increase on teenage labor demand and supply in the short term. — Tests the causal mechanism underlying the hypothesis (e.g., labor demand elasticity, substitution effects) and allows for counterfactual analysis under controlled assumptions, complementing empirical findings.

qualifier.temporal: in the short term (1–2 years after implementation)

C007.subject: raising the minimum wage in high-productivity sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in high-productivity sectors employee training investment per hire]

[PATH:empirical] BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation microdata, 2020-2024, focusing on high-productivity NAICS sectors (e.g., tech, finance, manufacturing) — Directly measures training expenditure per hire before and after minimum wage increases in targeted sectors, controlling for firm size and turnover.

[PATH:literature] Acemoglu & Pischke (1999) 'The Structure of Wages and Investment in General Training' and subsequent replication studies in US post-2020 data — Provides theoretical foundation for wage floors increasing employer-sponsored training due to reduced labor turnover; updated empirical tests can confirm or refute the hypothesis in high-productivity contexts.

[PATH:empirical] State-level minimum wage variation analysis (e.g., California vs. Texas) using QCEW and CPS data to isolate training investment per hire in high-productivity firms — Leverages quasi-experimental variation in minimum wage policies across states to identify causal effect on training investment, controlling for industry, productivity, and time trends.

C008.subject: raising the minimum wage in high-productivity sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in high-productivity sectors employee turnover costs]

[PATH:empirical] Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) data, segmented by industry (e.g., tech, finance) and wage tiers, 2010–present — Provides direct longitudinal data on quit rates and hiring costs in high-productivity sectors, allowing comparison before and after minimum wage increases to isolate effects on turnover costs.

[PATH:literature] Dube, A., Lester, T.W., & Reich, M. (2010). 'Minimum Wage Effects Across State Borders: Estimates Using Contiguous Counties.' Review of Economics and Statistics. — Classic empirical study using border discontinuity design; replicating with recent data and focusing on high-productivity sectors could test if turnover costs rise disproportionately in those sectors.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of efficiency wage and labor turnover dynamics (e.g., Shapiro & Stiglitz, 1984) applied to high-productivity firms — Predicts that higher minimum wages may reduce turnover by increasing worker attachment, contradicting the hypothesis; simulation with sector-specific parameters could clarify mechanisms.

C011.subject: raising the minimum wage in monopsonistic labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in monopsonistic labor markets firm-level investment in labor-saving technology]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on U.S. fast-food franchises (e.g., from Bureau of Labor Statistics or Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages) linked to state-level minimum wage increases, examining subsequent adoption of self-service kiosks or automated ordering systems — Directly tests whether minimum wage hikes in concentrated local labor markets (proxied by Herfindahl index) lead to increased automation investment, using difference-in-differences or event-study designs.

[PATH:empirical] European Union firm-level surveys (e.g., EIB Investment Survey or Community Innovation Survey) combined with national minimum wage reforms, focusing on manufacturing and retail sectors with moderate wage floors — Provides cross-country variation in monopsony power and wage floors, allowing estimation of heterogeneous effects on capital deepening, especially in industries with high labor-cost shares.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural model of monopsonistic competition with endogenous technology adoption (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo 2018 framework, calibrated to U.S. labor market data) — Simulates counterfactual minimum wage scenarios to isolate the causal mechanism—higher wages reduce labor demand elasticity, incentivizing automation—and generates testable predictions about firm size, market concentration, and investment thresholds.

scope.domain: monopsonistic labor markets with moderate wage floors

C012.subject: raising the minimum wage in monopsonistic labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in monopsonistic labor markets overall employment levels]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) study of fast-food employment in New Jersey and Pennsylvania after minimum wage increase — This classic natural experiment provides direct empirical evidence on employment effects in a context with potential monopsony power, challenging the standard competitive model and supporting the hypothesis that minimum wage may not reduce employment.

[PATH:theoretical] Bhaskar, Manning, and To (2002) 'Oligopsony and Monopsonistic Competition in Labor Markets' — This theoretical framework models how monopsonistic labor markets respond to minimum wage increases, predicting possible employment increases or minimal reductions, directly relevant to testing the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis by Doucouliagos and Stanley (2009) on minimum wage employment effects — A comprehensive meta-analysis of hundreds of studies can reveal the overall empirical consensus and heterogeneity, helping to confirm or refute whether the hypothesis holds under monopsonistic conditions.
